And yet most people do the very opposite of this: for when they have been prevented by some business from taking the morning meal, they think it right at dinner to recover also the nourishment omitted at the morning meal, not knowing that the body does indeed need the omitted nourishment, but that the stomach cannot work it up, having been harmed by the longer abstinence from food. Those, however, who are bitter-bilious in the upper parts themselves bear such things with more distress than the others.

Unit K15.753-754 (K. XV 753–754). ENGLISH:
I find that the ancient Greeks sometimes apply the name 'genus' also to things that are spoken of homonymously, whereas properly it belongs to things that have one signification but which, through the division made in accordance with it, arrive at several differentiae; in which case we are often accustomed to say that the generic differentiae of such-and-such a thing are two or three or four or as many as is possible. And since homonyms too are of two kinds—some having nothing at all in common with one another, as when we call both the dog on land (ἐπίπεδον) and the sea-dog 'dog', while others have something in common with synonyms, when they have their appellation derived from one single thing—one must further consider, as has been said, to which of these the two genera of causus are to be referred; and this will be known precisely from the account corresponding to the name, once the essence of each has been made clear. But since the account is judged by the conception, we must consider whether we possess a conception of the causus fever that is agreed upon in the same way as that of man and ox and horse; and since the discussion is likely to run out to a length greater than befits a commentary, we shall hasten to compress it, as we do the others too, into a brief summary, making this the starting point of the discussion.
